2027-07-14.title: Wednesday of the eighth week after Pentecost
readings: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth: you are God's field, God's building
Two blind men cry, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” and Jesus says, “According to your faith let it be done to you”
2027-07-14.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Eighth Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. Tomorrow, Thursday 15 July, is the commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios.
2027-07-14.verse: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.
theo: The Church at Corinth had split into parties. “What I mean is that each of you says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ or ‘I belong to Apollos,’ or ‘I belong to Cephas,’ or ‘I belong to Christ’” (1 Corinthians 1:12). Today St Paul answers with a picture that every farmer in Kerala understands: “What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you came to believe, as the Lord assigned to each. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.” In these weeks the seedlings of paddy are being transplanted into the flooded fields and the coconut saplings are going into the wet earth. Anyone who has done that work knows that the planter and the person who waters each have a task, and that both together cannot make a single seed grow. Life comes from God, and the servants are only servants. Paul does not make light of their labor: “The one who plants and the one who waters have a common purpose, and each will receive wages according to the labor of each.” The work is real, the reward is real, and the praise belongs to the Lord of the field.

Paul then gives two pictures of the Church: “For we are God's servants, working together; you are God's field, God's building.” A field and a building: a field that must be tended, patiently, season after season; a building that is raised stone upon stone. He goes on to say that he himself laid a foundation and another is building on it, and that “no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid; that foundation is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:10–11). The faith we received in India was planted and watered by many hands: the Apostle Thomas, according to tradition, who first sowed the Gospel on our shores; the mothers who taught prayers; the priests who kept the Qurbono alive in hard times. Tomorrow the Church of the Syro-Malankara tradition remembers one of those planters, Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who died on 15 July 1953. He founded the Bethany Ashram in 1919 and the Bethany Sisters in 1925, was received with Mar Theophilos and their companions into full communion with the Catholic Church on 20 September 1930, keeping the Syriac liturgy of the Malankara tradition, and in 1932 became the first Archbishop of Trivandrum. He planted in poverty and in tears, and the growth, in eparchies across India and beyond, has been God's. Tonight is a good evening to thank him, and to ask which part of the field has been given to us to plant or to water.

The Gospel brings us two men who could not see. “As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying loudly, ‘Have mercy on us, Son of David!’” They cannot see the road, but they see who he is, for “Son of David” is the title of the promised Messiah, and the prophet had said that “the eyes of the blind shall be opened” (Isaiah 35:5). They follow him all the way into a house, and there Jesus asks them one question: “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They said to him, “Yes, Lord.” “Then he touched their eyes and said, ‘According to your faith let it be done to you.’ And their eyes were opened.” Faith here is not a payment that buys a miracle; it is an open hand. Then Jesus sternly orders them: “See that no one knows of this.” Probably he wished to avoid becoming a mere wonder-worker before his hour had come. But the two men “went away and spread the news about him throughout that district.” Their gratitude was too great to keep quiet. The cry of the blind men is the cry that rises in every Holy Qurbono: Lord, have mercy. And like the Corinthians whose eyes were dim with party spirit, we too need our eyes opened to see that all growth is God's gift, and that we are one field, one building, one body in the one Lord.
outline: Ask: who planted or watered the faith in me, and what part of the field has been given to me?
Paul and Apollos are servants; the one who plants and the one who waters are nothing without God.
The Church is tended season after season, with Jesus Christ as the only foundation; the eve of the commemoration of Mar Ivanios.
Two blind men who see who Jesus is before they see his face; faith is an open hand; they cannot keep silent.
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”
live: Thank by name someone who planted or watered the faith in you, by a call, a prayer or a visit, and say a prayer for Archbishop Mar Ivanios tonight.
Choose one small piece of the Church's field, a class, a visit, a cleaning, a collection, and do it faithfully this week.
Pray the cry of the blind men slowly three times each day: “Lord Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on us.”
2027-07-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the only foundation, and from you comes all growth. We thank you for those who planted and watered the faith in our land, and especially for Archbishop Mar Ivanios, whose memory we shall keep tomorrow. Make us faithful servants in your field, glad to plant and glad to water, and never proud of the harvest. Open our eyes, as you opened the eyes of the two blind men, to see you and to see one another as members of one building. Lord, have mercy on us. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the Church is built on the one foundation, Jesus Christ; we come as the blind men came into the house, crying for mercy, and the Lord touches our eyes and feeds us.

quick: St Paul says: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth; we are God's field and God's building.
Tomorrow the Church remembers Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who planted in poverty what has grown through God's gift.
Two blind men cry, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!” and Jesus opens their eyes according to their faith.
2027-07-14.action: Thank, today, one person who planted or watered your faith; and say, “Lord, have mercy on us,” three times.
2027-07-14.question: Do I plant and water in the Lord's field, or do I only look for the harvest?

family.explain: A farmer plants the seed and waters it, but he cannot make it grow; only God does that. St Paul says we are all workers in God's field. Some plant, some water, and God gives the growth. In the Gospel two blind men cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us!” and Jesus opened their eyes because they believed. When we ask Jesus for help with a believing heart, he hears us.
family.intention: We thank God for those who taught us to pray, and we pray for the Church founded by Archbishop Mar Ivanios, whose memory we keep tomorrow.
family.ask: Ask: “Who planted the faith in us? Let us name them and thank God tonight.”

illus: An old man in a village near Kottarakkara was seen one rainy morning planting a coconut sapling in his compound. A neighbour smiled and said that he would never taste a nut from that tree: it would not bear for seven years, and he was past eighty. The old man went on with his work. He said: I have eaten from my grandfather's trees all my life, and I never once thanked him to his face. Somebody must plant for those who come after. This is the only way I know to say thank you. Years later his grandsons, sitting under the same tree on the day of the first harvest, told the story to their own children.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, only foundation of your Church, from you comes all growth. Make us faithful in planting and in watering, and open our eyes to see you. Amen.
share: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Who planted or watered my faith?
You are God's field, God's building (1 Corinthians 3:9). What part of the field has been given to me?
According to your faith let it be done to you (Matthew 9:29). What do I ask of Jesus with an open hand?
interc: For the Church, God's field and God's building, that she may grow in unity on the one foundation, Jesus Christ.
For the Syro-Malankara Church on the eve of the commemoration of Archbishop Mar Ivanios, and for the unity of all Christians.
For those who cannot see, in body or in heart, that the Lord may open their eyes.
For farmers planting in this monsoon, and for all who work for a harvest they may not see.
For our parish, that each of us may do our own part and give the glory to God.
pm.close: Father, you give the growth to all that is planted in your name. Bless the labor of those who plant and water in your Church, open our eyes to see your hand in all things, and bring us all to your harvest. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, St Paul speaks to a divided community: some said, I belong to Paul, and others, I belong to Apollos. And Paul answers with a picture from the field: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). In these weeks of rain, our fields are being planted. We know that no farmer makes the seed grow. He prepares the soil, he plants, he waters, and then he waits for God.

Paul adds: you are God's field, God's building (1 Corinthians 3:9). A field needs care in every season; a building rises stone by stone. The faith we have received was planted and watered by many hands that we never saw: the Apostle Thomas, the first Christians of our land, parents and grandparents, priests who kept the Qurbono alive. Tomorrow the Church remembers Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who died on 15 July 1953. He worked and prayed for the unity of the Church and for the Malankara tradition, and he began in poverty. What he planted has grown, and the growth is God's.

In the Gospel, two blind men follow Jesus, crying, Have mercy on us, Son of David! (Matthew 9:27). They could not see the road, but they saw who he was. Jesus asks them: Do you believe that I am able to do this? Yes, Lord, they say. And he touches their eyes: According to your faith let it be done to you (Matthew 9:29). Faith is an open hand that receives. And when they were healed, they could not keep silent about him.

So tonight, let us thank someone who planted our faith. Let us do our part in the field faithfully, and give the glory to the Lord who gives the growth. And let us say, with the blind men, Lord, have mercy on us. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever planted a seed and watered it every day? You cannot make the seed grow yourself; only God does that. But you plant it and you water it, and God does the rest. St Paul says that we are all workers in God's garden: some plant, some water, and God makes it grow. Somebody planted our faith: our grandparents, our parents, the priests, the catechism teachers. Tomorrow we remember Archbishop Mar Ivanios, who planted something very important in our Church. In the Gospel two men who were blind cried, Jesus, have mercy on us! And Jesus opened their eyes. This week, plant something small, a seed or a flower, and water it, and say a thank-you prayer for the people who planted your faith.

The cry Have mercy on us opens our eyes to see his hand in all the growth we have received.
